newsitem.title: ISRAEL: First Int'l Bank Q4 EPS 8.46 shekels.
newsitem.headline: First Int'l Bank Q4 EPS 8.46 shekels.

text.p: First International Bank of Israel.
(in millions of shekels, except EPS)
Income before
Debt provision 11.2 16.9 57.5 62.0
Operating, other
Earnings per share 8.46 8.04 35.01 31.76
First International, Israel's fourth-largest bank, said net return on equity (ROE) was 9.2 percent for all of 1996, compared with 8.7 percent in 1995.

The bank unofficially reported results in dollar terms, which Managing Director Shlomo Piotrkowsky said was intended to help overseas investors. It showed net rising 32 percent for the year to $130.7 million, giving First International a net ROE of 15.6 percent.
Credit to the public grew 16.2 percent last year to 22.2 billion shekels. Deposits from the public rose 16.5 percent to 25.4 billion shekels, First International said.

Shareholders equity reached 1.99 billion shekels at the end of last year, compared with 1.91 billion shekels at the end of 1995. Total assets rose 17.1 percent to 32.0 billion shekels at the end of 1996.
First International said the 1.8 percent increase in financial income was due to increased lending activity. It added that financial margins were stable over the course of year.

Operating income was ahead 9.7 percent for the year, which the bank attributed to increased customer transactions, mainly in foreign currency trading. This, the bank said, was offset by reduced activity in the capital market last year and by a real decline in fees.
The bank said net earnings were helped by inflationary accounting, which added 6.6 million shekels to earnings.

First International declared an aggregate dividend of 101 million shekels. In addition, the bank said it would be paying clients 15 million shekels as part of its four-year-old profit-sharing programme.
Piotrkowsky said one of the most important changes occuring in the banking sector was the growing role of foreign currency and foreign currency-linked borrowing.
He said forex and forex-linked loans now accounted for 33 percent of the lending portfolios of Israel's seven banking groups, up from 20 percent three years ago.
"We are witnessing a a basic and structural change in everything connected with the structure of credit in the (banking) system," Piotrkowski said.
Real interest rates on dollar loans, First International said, were close to nil last year, compared with nine percent on shekel loans not linked to the consumer price index.

Piotrkowsky said borrowers were counting on a stable shekel-dollar exchange rate. He warned that these borrowers, most of whom did not have forex income or assets, were exposing themselves to possible sharp fluctuations in the exchange rate.
